standard_text: Apply the order of operations and properties of operations (i.e., identity, inverse, commutative properties of addition and multiplication, associative properties of addition and multiplication, and distributive property) to evaluate numerical expressions with nonnegative rational numbers, including those using grouping symbols, such as parentheses, and involving whole number exponents.

progression.narrative: 6.NS.5 hands students a numerical expression and asks one thing: evaluate it the way every mathematician on Earth would -- same steps, same answer. Two tool kits make that possible. The order of operations says WHICH step runs first, and the standard builds that demand in layers: first a single set of parentheses with whole numbers (S1), then nested brackets and multiple operations where the same-rank left-to-right rule for multiplication and division earns its keep (S3), then whole-number exponents -- including zero -- mixed with fractions and decimals (S4). The properties of operations are the second kit: the legal moves that rewrite an expression without changing its value. Students first learn to NAME the move an equation shows (S2), then to USE the biggest one -- the distributive property -- to build equivalent expressions themselves (S5). The capstone runs the whole standard in reverse: given a target value, students place the grouping symbols or judge a lineup of candidate expressions, which only works if evaluating (S1-S4) and rewriting (S2, S5) have both become instinct (S6).

steps.rationale: The standard's core demand at its simplest: one set of parentheses, whole numbers. This is where the left-to-right reading habit first collides with the rules -- and must lose.
The standard names the properties of operations explicitly. Before students can USE a property to rewrite an expression, they must recognize which legal move an equation is showing.
The item spec's medium tier: nested grouping and multiple operations inside one layer. The multiplication/division same-rank rule -- hidden at S1's difficulty -- becomes unavoidable here.
The standard's full evaluation demand: whole-number exponents (including zero) joining fractions and decimals. The exponent is the one genuinely new symbol grade 6 adds to the order.

From naming to using: the distributive property rewrites an expression without changing its value -- the move the spec's equivalent-expression items test and the bridge from S2's recognition to S6's production.

The above-proficiency reversal: place grouping symbols to hit a target value and judge candidate equivalents. Doing this requires evaluating AND rewriting on demand -- the whole standard, run backward.

skills.name: Recall multiplication and division facts fluently

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply and divide single-digit numbers from memory

skills.i_do_script: Every order-of-operations problem is really a chain of small facts -- 42 divided by 7, 6 times 6 -- and each one has to come fast so your brain can focus on the ORDER, not the arithmetic. If a fact isn't automatic, we build it from one you do know: 6 x 7 is one more group of 6 than 6 x 6 = 36, so it's 42. Division facts are just multiplication facts read backward: 54 / 6 asks '6 times what is 54?'

canonical_error.pattern: Cannot recall multiplication or division facts, so errors cascade into every expression
canonical_error.example: Inside 6 x (42 / 7) + 100, the student computes 42 / 7 = 7 instead of 6, and everything after is wrong
canonical_error.why: Facts weren't automatized in grades 3-4. The student may know exactly which step comes first but can't execute it reliably, so order-of-operations practice keeps failing for arithmetic reasons.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- let's double-check that fact.
redirect_script.prompt: Use a fact you trust to reach the one you need. For 42 / 7, ask '7 times what makes 42?' Count up by 7s if you need to: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 -- that's six 7s.
redirect_script.praise: You rebuilt the fact from one you knew. That's exactly how fluency grows.

skills.item_template: A single multiplication or division fact (facts through 12). NR (numeric response). No context, no grouping symbols -- just the fact.

The answer you get when you divide one number by another.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S1: evaluate expressions with one set of parentheses. The facts are ready -- now the order matters.
next_steps.if_fail: Run short daily fact sprints (2 minutes, facts through 9) before any expression work. Rebuild missing facts from anchor facts the student trusts.

worked_example_script.text: Here's the fact: 6 x 7. Is that one you just know, or do you need a second to build it?
If it's not automatic, name a 6-times fact you DO trust that's close to 6 x 7.
Say you picked 6 x 6. What does 6 x 6 equal?
6 x 7 is how many more groups of 6 than 6 x 6?
One more group. So what do you do to 36 to get 6 x 7?
If they say 48, they jumped to 6 x 8. Ask: 'How many groups of 6 are in 6 x 7?' If they say 36, they forgot to add the extra group -- point at the 7 and ask, 'Did we add that last group of 6 yet?'
36 + 6 = 42, so 6 x 7 = 42. And that means 42 / 7 = 6 and 42 / 6 = 7 -- one fact, three ways to use it.
Your turn: use the same move to build 8 x 9 from 8 x 8.

skills.name: Compute with simple fractions and decimals

prerequisite_skill.description: Add, subtract, and multiply simple fractions and decimals

skills.i_do_script: The hardest 6.NS.5 problems mix fractions and decimals into the expressions, so the small computations have to be solid first. Watch me do one: 1/2 + 1/4. Halves and fourths aren't the same size piece, so I trade the 1/2 for 2/4 -- now 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. With decimals, I line up the decimal points: 2.5 + 1.7 is 25 tenths plus 17 tenths, which is 42 tenths -- 4.2.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds fraction pieces or decimal digits without matching sizes -- adds numerators AND denominators, or misaligns decimal points
canonical_error.why: The student treats the two parts of a fraction (or the digits of a decimal) as separate whole numbers instead of as one quantity, so they combine pieces that aren't the same size.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- are those pieces the same size?
redirect_script.prompt: Before adding fractions, make the denominators match: trade 1/2 for 2/4 first. For decimals, stack the numbers so the decimal points line up, then add.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the piece sizes first -- that's the whole trick.

skills.item_template: A single operation on two simple fractions (denominators 2, 3, 4, 5) or one-place decimals. NR response. All values nonnegative.

Common error: 2/2 from subtracting numerators and denominators separately

vocabulary.definition: The top number of a fraction -- how many pieces you have.
The bottom number of a fraction -- how big each piece is (how many make a whole).

next_steps.if_pass: The student can handle the rational-number arithmetic inside 6NS5-S4's harder expressions. Continue the main progression.
next_steps.if_fail: Practice matching denominators with fraction strips and lining up decimal points on grid paper before returning to expressions with fractions or decimals.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 1/2 + 1/4.
If I hand you half a sandwich and a quarter of a sandwich, can you just count '1 piece plus 1 piece = 2 pieces'? Why not?
The pieces are different sizes. How could we cut the half so ALL the pieces are the same size?
Right -- a half is the same as two fourths. So what does the problem look like now, written all in fourths?
2/4 + 1/4 -- now the pieces match. How many fourths in all?
If the student says 3/8, they added the denominators. Ask: 'Did the SIZE of the pieces change when we combined them, or just the count?'
Three fourths. The denominator names the piece size, and it stays put -- only the count on top adds.
Your turn: 3/5 + 1/5. Same-size pieces already? Then how many fifths?

skills.name: Evaluate expressions with one set of parentheses and whole numbers
skills.i_do_script: An expression is a story squeezed onto one line. Here's this one's story: 42 kids share 7 vans equally, 6 vans of that size arrive at the museum, and 100 more kids walk. The story forces an order -- you can't count the riders before you know how many kids fit per van -- and the symbols simply record that forced order. We're going to evaluate an expression that mixes operations, like 6 x (42 / 7) + 100. The parentheses are the author of the problem telling us 'do THIS piece first.' Watch: 42 / 7 = 6, so the expression becomes 6 x 6 + 100. Then multiplication beats addition: 36 + 100 = 136. The one rule I'll keep asking about: which step does the expression let you do first?

canonical_error.pattern: Works strictly left to right, ignoring parentheses and the priority of multiplication and division over addition and subtraction
canonical_error.example: For 60 - 5 x 8, computes 60 - 5 = 55 first, then 55 x 8 = 440, instead of 5 x 8 = 40, then 60 - 40 = 20
canonical_error.why: Reading habits transfer from text: we read left to right, so students compute left to right. They haven't internalized that math expressions are read by RULE (grouping first, then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction), not by position.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- did you check what comes first?
redirect_script.prompt: Go back to the van story: which amount does the story force you to find first? Circle the parentheses first, then underline any multiplication or division. Those steps happen BEFORE adding or subtracting, no matter where they sit in the line. Now which piece do you compute first?
redirect_script.praise: You found the first step by rule, not by position. That's exactly how order of operations works.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression with whole numbers, one set of parentheses containing one operation, and one or two operations outside. Student evaluates. NR response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 352 from left-to-right (6 x 42 = 252, / 7 = 36, + 100 = 136 accidentally works here for some paths; the true trap is adding 7 + 100 first) or ignoring the parentheses entirely
Common error: 40 from adding 5 + 3 first, then multiplying by 5
Common error: subtracting 3 - 10 is blocked, so students may compute 8 + 4 x 3 = 20 by dropping the parentheses
Common error: 532 from computing 40 - 2 = 38 first, then 38 x 14

vocabulary.definition: A math phrase made of numbers and operations. It shows a value but has no equals sign.
The agreed rules for which step to compute first: grouping symbols, then exponents, then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction.
Parentheses ( ) or brackets [ ] that fence off the part of the expression to compute first.
Work an expression all the way down to a single number.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S3: nested grouping symbols with two operations inside. Same rules, deeper layers.
next_steps.if_fail: Check 6NS5-F1 (fact fluency). If facts are solid, re-teach with the circle-the-parentheses routine and one-step-per-line recording.

worked_example_script.text: Tell the story behind 6 x (42 / 7) + 100 before computing anything: 42 kids split equally among 7 vans -- that's the (42 / 7) chunk. Then 6 vans of that size arrive, and 100 more kids walk. The whole expression counts kids at the museum.

Try reading it like a book, left to right: could you compute 6 x 42 first? What would 252 even count in this story, before the splitting into 7 vans has happened? And could you add the 100 walkers before you know how many kids rode? Which piece does the STORY force you to settle first?

The story computes itself from the inside out: kids per van first (42 / 7 = 6), then the riders (6 x 6 = 36), then everybody (36 + 100 = 136). Parentheses and operation ranks are just the written record of the order the story already demanded.
Write on the board: 6 x (42 / 7) + 100.
Before we compute anything -- what do the parentheses tell us?
So which small problem do we do first, and what does it equal?
Cross out (42 / 7) and write 6 above it. The board now reads: 6 x 6 + 100.
Two operations left: a multiplication and an addition. Which one wins, and why?
If the student wants to add 6 + 100 first because 'it's next to it,' pause. Ask: 'Are we reading like a book, or following the math rules? Which operation ranks higher?'
So 6 x 6 = 36, and then what's the final step and the final answer?
36 + 100 = 136. Notice we rewrote the expression after every single step -- one step per line keeps the order honest.

practice_problems.answer: 20. Multiplication comes before subtraction: 5 x 8 = 40, then 60 - 40 = 20.
practice_problems.notes: The left-to-right-over-PEMDAS bait. Ask what RULE decides the first step, not what position.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate 7 + 2 x (10 - 6). Then mark your answer on the number line.

practice_problems.notes: Multiplication AND division both beat subtraction; students must hold two first-tier results (18 and 3).

practice_problems.stem: Write your own expression that uses one set of parentheses and equals exactly 20. Prove it by evaluating, one step per line.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct expression, e.g. 4 x (2 + 3) = 4 x 5 = 20, or (30 - 10) / 1 = 20.

activities.title: The Left-to-Right Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read DeShawn's work silently and mark the exact line where it went wrong.
2. Ask: why did DeShawn's way FEEL right? (We read everything else left to right.)
3. Pairs redo the problem with one step per line, saying the rule that picks each step.
4. Debrief: what's the difference between how we read words and how we read math?

content.error_step: DeShawn subtracted first because it came first reading left to right.
content.why: Multiplication outranks subtraction no matter where it sits: 5 x 8 = 40 happens first, then 60 - 40 = 20.

activities.title: What Comes First?
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the three headers: 'Parentheses first,' 'Multiply/divide first,' 'Add/subtract first (nothing outranks it).'
2. Groups sort each expression card by which KIND of step comes first.
3. A card only stays placed when the group names the actual first computation out loud.
4. Debrief with the two cards that look alike but sort differently: 5 + 3 x 2 vs (5 + 3) x 2.

activities.title: First Step Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Project an expression like 40 - 2 x (6 + 8).
2. Students write ONLY the first step (the piece they'd compute first) -- not the answer.
3. On 'show,' everyone reveals at once. One student defends the majority choice, one defends any different choice.
4. Then evaluate the whole expression together, one step per line. Score a class point when the room agrees on the first step immediately.

strategy_links.why: Pairing a correct worked example with DeShawn's left-to-right version makes the rule-vs-position contrast the lesson itself.
Whiteboard rounds on 'first step only' reveal instantly who is still computing by position.
Thinking aloud -- 'parentheses first, then I scan for multiply or divide' -- models the scan students must automate.

questioning_prompts: Before you touch a number: what does the expression LET you do first, and what rule says so?
You computed a step -- rewrite the whole expression with that step's answer in its place. What does the line say now?
Where would the answer change if I erased the parentheses? Try it both ways.
Why do you think mathematicians agreed on one order instead of letting everyone read left to right?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes left to right -- e.g., 60 - 5 first in 60 - 5 x 8 -- ignoring operation priority.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the parentheses first, then underline any multiplication or division. Those steps happen BEFORE adding or subtracting, no matter where they sit in the line. Now which piece do you compute first?
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the first step by rule, not by position. That's exactly how order of operations works.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student does the parentheses but then skips a step, combining two operations in one line and losing track.
misconception_redirects.say: One step per line. Compute exactly one piece, rewrite everything else unchanged, and read the new line fresh.
misconception_redirects.praise: Every line of your work is a true statement -- that's what clean evaluation looks like.

quick_checks.prompt: Don't solve it -- just tell me the FIRST step in 7 + 2 x (10 - 6).
quick_checks.look_for: '10 - 6.' Answering '7 + 2' means position is still beating rule; answering '2 x 10' means the parentheses are invisible to them.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: in 30 - 12 / 4, you subtract first because it comes first.
quick_checks.look_for: False, with the reason -- division outranks subtraction, so 12 / 4 = 3 happens first and the answer is 27. 'True' means the canonical error is live.

sentence_starters: The first step is ___ because the rule says ___ comes before ___.
After that step, my new line reads ___.

steps.annotation: Scan before you compute: parentheses first, always.
42 / 7 = 6. Rewrite the whole line with 6 standing in for the parentheses.
Multiplication beats addition, even though the + 100 is sitting right there.
Only when multiplication is done does the addition get its turn.
Parentheses first: 15 - 9 = 6.
Which operation wins now -- the multiplication or the addition? Compute it and rewrite the line.
Finish with the last operation.

skills.name: Identify the property of operations shown by an equation
skills.i_do_script: Two expressions can look different but be worth exactly the same amount, and the properties of operations are the legal moves that get you from one to the other. Watch me read 9 + 5 = 5 + 9: the numbers SWAPPED places -- that's the commutative property. Now (5 + 2) + 8 = 5 + (2 + 8): the numbers stayed in order and only the parentheses moved -- that's the associative property. The question I'll keep asking: what MOVED?

canonical_error.pattern: Labels any rearranged equation 'commutative' -- cannot distinguish numbers swapping places from parentheses moving
canonical_error.example: Calls (5 + 2) + 8 = 5 + (2 + 8) the commutative property because 'the numbers moved around'
canonical_error.why: The student sees that the two sides look different and reaches for the one property name they remember. They haven't isolated WHAT changed: commutative changes the ORDER of the numbers; associative changes only the GROUPING while the order stays fixed.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- let's check what actually moved.
redirect_script.prompt: Read the numbers on each side in order and write them down: left side, then right side. Same order? Then the numbers didn't move -- only the parentheses did, and that's associative. Different order? That's commutative.
redirect_script.praise: You tracked what moved instead of guessing the name. That's the whole skill.

skills.item_template: An equation demonstrating one property (commutative, associative, distributive, identity, or inverse) with whole numbers. Student selects the property name. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem:
Which property of operations is shown by the equation below?

9 + 5 = 5 + 9
sample_items.distractor_logic: Associative -- student confuses swapping order with regrouping; Distributive -- grabs the longest name

sample_items.stem:
Which property of operations is shown by the equation below?

(2 x 3) x 4 = 2 x (3 x 4)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Commutative -- the canonical error: student sees rearrangement and defaults to commutative even though the factor order never changed

sample_items.stem:
Which property of operations is shown by the equation below?

7 x (10 + 2) = 7 x 10 + 7 x 2
sample_items.distractor_logic: Associative -- student sees parentheses and assumes regrouping; commutative -- default guess

sample_items.stem:
Which property of operations is shown by the equation below?

(6 + 1) + 9 = 6 + (1 + 9)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Commutative -- the canonical error; the addend order (6, 1, 9) is identical on both sides

vocabulary.definition: You can swap the ORDER of the numbers when adding or multiplying: a + b = b + a.
You can move the parentheses (the GROUPING) when adding or multiplying: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). The order stays the same.
A number outside parentheses multiplies EVERY term inside: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c.
Adding 0 or multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged: n + 0 = n and n x 1 = n.
A number and its opposite partner undo each other: 3/4 x 4/3 = 1, and 5 + (-5) = 0 (in grade 6 we focus on the multiplication version).

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S5: USE the distributive property to write equivalent expressions, not just name it.
next_steps.if_fail: Re-teach with the 'what moved?' routine: write the numbers of each side in order and compare before naming anything.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 9 + 5 = 5 + 9.
Read the left side's numbers in order, then the right side's. Write both lists -- 9, 5 and 5, 9. Did the numbers keep their order, or trade places?
They traded places -- 9 and 5 swapped spots. When the ORDER of the numbers changes but the value stays the same, which property is that?

Watch for a student who names a property without checking what moved -- guessing 'associative' because there are two sides, or blurting 'commutative' with no reason. Have them read each side's numbers in order: left is 9, 5; right is 5, 9, so the numbers themselves swapped -- that's commutative. Write (5 + 2) + 8 = 5 + (2 + 8) beside it, where the numbers stay 5, 2, 8 and only the grouping moves, to show what associative looks like instead.
Now prove both sides really are equal. What does 9 + 5 give, and what does 5 + 9 give?
14 both ways. Commutative property of addition: the order flipped, but the sum never changed -- that's exactly what the property promises.
Your turn: 4 x 7 = 7 x 4. What moved, and what's the property?

practice_problems.stem: Which property is shown? 4 + 9 = 9 + 4
Which property is shown? 3 x 8 = 8 x 3
Which property is shown? (7 + 5) + 3 = 7 + (5 + 3)
practice_problems.notes: The commutative-by-default trap: the addend order never changes.

practice_problems.stem: Which property is shown? 6 x (20 + 4) = 6 x 20 + 6 x 4
Marcus named the property shown by (5 + 2) + 8 = 5 + (2 + 8). Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marcus wrote: commutative property of addition, because the numbers moved around
practice_problems.answer: Associative property of addition. The numbers stayed in the same order (5, 2, 8 on both sides) -- only the parentheses moved. Commutative means the numbers themselves swap places, like 5 + 8 = 8 + 5.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical commutative-vs-associative confusion.

practice_problems.stem: Which property is shown? 15 x 1 = 15
Which property is shown? 3/4 x 4/3 = 1
practice_problems.notes: Multiplying by the reciprocal 'undoes' back to 1 -- the multiplication version of an inverse.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own equation that shows the distributive property, then evaluate both sides to prove they match.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct equation, e.g. 3 x (10 + 2) = 3 x 10 + 3 x 2; both sides equal 36.
practice_problems.notes: Producing an example shows ownership beyond recognition.

activities.title: What Moved? Property Sort
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the headers: Commutative, Associative, Distributive, Identity.
2. For each equation card, partners must first answer 'what moved?' out loud (numbers swapped / parentheses moved / a number got shared out / nothing changed) BEFORE placing it.
3. Challenge rule: a partner can force a re-check by asking for the numbers of each side read in order.
4. Debrief on the pair of cards that look most alike but land in different columns.

activities.title: Why Did Marcus Say Commutative?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Marcus's work. Ask first: what was Marcus thinking? (Something DID move -- his instinct wasn't crazy.)
2. Groups write the numbers of each side in order and compare the two lists.
3. Each group states the one-sentence test that separates commutative from associative.
4. Exit: every student writes Marcus a tip that starts with 'Check whether...'

content.error_step: Marcus saw the two sides looked different and grabbed 'commutative' without checking WHAT changed.
content.why: The addends stay in the order 5, 2, 8 on both sides -- only the grouping moved, which is the associative property. Commutative requires the numbers themselves to swap.

activities.title: Property Choral Rounds
activities.instructions:
1. Display an equation for 5 seconds.
2. On the signal, the class answers together with just the property's first word: 'commutative!', 'associative!', 'distributive!', 'identity!'
3. After each round, one random student gives the because-sentence: 'because the ___ moved.'
4. Speed up as accuracy holds; recycle any equation that splits the room.

strategy_links.why: 'What moved?' is a perfect 30-second pair discussion before any property gets named.
Marcus's commutative-for-everything answer is the exact misconception worth dissecting as a group.
Choral property naming builds the fast, confident vocabulary recall this identification skill needs.

questioning_prompts: Read the numbers on each side in order. Are the two lists the same or different?
What moved in this equation -- the numbers, the parentheses, or did a number get shared out to everything inside?
Both sides of this equation -- are they actually equal? Prove it by evaluating each side.
Give me a commutative example and an associative example that use the SAME three numbers. What's the only difference?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls an associative equation 'commutative' because 'the numbers moved around.'
misconception_redirects.say: Read the numbers on each side in order and write them down: left side, then right side. Same order? Then the numbers didn't move -- only the parentheses did, and that's associative. Different order? That's commutative.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tracked what moved instead of guessing the name. That's the whole skill.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls any equation with parentheses 'distributive,' even pure regrouping like (2 x 5) x 8 = 2 x (5 x 8).
misconception_redirects.say: Distributive needs TWO different operations -- a multiplication reaching in across an addition or subtraction. Is there an addition inside these parentheses being multiplied, or is it multiplication all the way through?
misconception_redirects.praise: Exactly -- distributive is the only property that mixes two operations. You checked for that.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up if this is associative: 8 + 3 = 3 + 8.
quick_checks.look_for: Thumbs DOWN (it's commutative -- the numbers swapped). A thumbs up means the two properties are still one blur.

quick_checks.prompt: Fill in the blank so this shows the identity property: 47 x ___ = 47.
quick_checks.look_for: 1. An answer of 0 means the student is thinking of the addition identity -- probe whether they know why the two identities differ.

sentence_starters: The ___ moved, so this is the ___ property.
I know it is NOT commutative because the numbers stayed in the order ___.

steps.annotation: One 7 multiplying a package of two terms.
The 7 got handed to EACH term inside -- shared out, or 'distributed.'

skills.name: Evaluate expressions with nested grouping symbols and multiple operations
skills.i_do_script: Here's the story hiding in the layers: 54 stickers shared equally by 9 kids, then 14 bonus stickers handed to each kid, then each kid splits their whole pile evenly across 4 album pages. You can't hand out bonuses before the shares exist, and you can't fill pages before the piles are complete -- the story runs inside-out, and the brackets record it. Now the expressions have layers: brackets on the outside, parentheses on the inside, like [(54 / 9 + 14) / 4]. We work from the INSIDE out: 54 / 9 = 6 first, then 6 + 14 = 20 inside the parentheses, then 20 / 4 = 5 for the brackets. One more rule to lock in: multiplication and division are the SAME rank -- inside any layer you take them left to right, never 'multiplication always first.'

canonical_error.pattern: Believes multiplication always comes before division because M comes before D in PEMDAS
canonical_error.example: For 36 / 6 x 2, computes 6 x 2 = 12 first and gets 36 / 12 = 3, instead of working left to right: 36 / 6 = 6, then 6 x 2 = 12
canonical_error.why: The student reads the PEMDAS acronym as six separate ranked steps. In reality it has four tiers -- multiplication/division share a tier and are worked left to right, as do addition/subtraction. The acronym's letter order creates the false hierarchy.

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- M and D are teammates, not ranked.
redirect_script.prompt: Think of the sticker story: sharing out and scaling up are the same kind of resize move -- they happen in the order they come, left to right. Multiplication and division are the same step. When both appear, sweep left to right like reading. Put your finger on the leftmost x or / and do that one first.
redirect_script.praise: You swept left to right through the same-rank operations. That's the rule most people miss.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression with whole numbers, two operations inside grouping symbols or two sets of grouping symbols (parentheses inside brackets). Student evaluates. NR or MC response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 9.5 from adding 9 + 14 first inside; 16 from mishandling the outer division
Common error: 3 x 6 - 8 x 2 = 2 if grouping is dropped; or subtracting 6 - 8 is blocked so student reorders arbitrarily
Common error: 20 + 4 = 24 first (left to right), giving 24 x 7 - 15 = 153
Common error: 30 / (5 + 9) path from grouping confusion, or 30 / 5 + 9 / 3 = 9 from splitting the outer division

vocabulary.definition: Square grouping symbols [ ] that usually wrap around parentheses to show an outer layer.
Grouping symbols inside other grouping symbols. Work from the innermost pair outward.
Grouping symbols, then exponents, then multiplication/division left to right, then addition/subtraction left to right.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S4: add whole-number exponents and fraction/decimal values to the mix.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to 6NS5-S1 for single-layer grouping, then re-introduce nesting with the inside-out highlighting routine.

worked_example_script.text: Map [(54 / 9 + 14) / 4] to its story before computing: 54 stickers shared by 9 kids (the 54 / 9), plus 14 bonus stickers each (the + 14), and then each kid spreads their whole pile across 4 album pages (the outer / 4).
Could you do the + 14 first? What would 14 be added TO, before each kid's share of the 54 even exists? Which piece does the story force you to settle before anything else can happen?

The story runs inside-out on its own: 54 / 9 = 6 stickers each, plus 14 makes 20, spread over 4 pages is 5 per page. And notice sharing out (dividing) and scaling up (multiplying) are the same kind of resize move in the story -- neither one outranks the other; they just happen in the order they come.
Write on the board: [(54 / 9 + 14) / 4].
There are two layers of grouping here. Which layer do we open first -- the brackets or the parentheses inside them?
Inside the parentheses there are two operations: a division and an addition. Which happens first, and why?

If the student adds 9 + 14 first, ask: 'Inside a grouping symbol, do the ranking rules still apply, or does everything become equal?' The rules apply everywhere -- division beats addition even inside parentheses.
So 54 / 9 = 6. Rewrite the inside. What does the parentheses layer say now?
6 + 14 = 20, so the parentheses collapse to 20. What's left inside the brackets?
20 / 4 -- what's the final answer?

5. Inside out, one layer at a time, and the ranking rules never turn off. One more thing to remember for expressions like 36 / 6 x 2: multiplication and division are the same rank -- sweep left to right.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: (12 - 4) / 2
Evaluate: [6 + (2 x 5)]

practice_problems.notes: Division-then-addition inside, division outside. Watch for 24 / 6 + 8 / 2 = 8 -- splitting the outer division.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: 48 / 6 x 2
practice_problems.notes: Same-rank sweep: 48 / 6 = 8, then 8 x 2 = 16. The multiply-first crowd gets 4.

practice_problems.stem: Keisha evaluated 36 / 6 x 2. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: = 36 / 12   (did the multiplication first, because M comes before D in PEMDAS)
practice_problems.answer: 12. Multiplication and division are the SAME rank, worked left to right: 36 / 6 = 6, then 6 x 2 = 12.
practice_problems.notes: The multiply-before-divide-always bait. Ask: does the acronym's spelling outrank the left-to-right rule?

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: [(5 x 8 - 10) / 6]
practice_problems.notes: Multiply, then subtract, then the outer division: (40 - 10) / 6 = 30 / 6.
Two separate parentheses feeding one division: 24 / 6.
The whole bracket resolves to 50 before the subtraction touches anything: 4 x 5 = 20, + 30 = 50, then 100 - 50.

activities.title: Does M Really Beat D?
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Keisha's work and mark where it went wrong.
2. Ask: what did Keisha believe about PEMDAS? (Her reading of the acronym is the interesting part.)
3. Pairs redo 36 / 6 x 2 with a left-to-right finger sweep, then invent one more expression where multiply-first gives the wrong answer.
4. Debrief: how would you rewrite PEMDAS so nobody makes Keisha's mistake? (e.g., four tiers, or GEMS.)

content.worked_problem: 36 / 6 x 2. Keisha wrote: 6 x 2 = 12 first, then 36 / 12 = 3.
content.error_step: Keisha did the multiplication before the division because M comes before D in the acronym.
content.why: Multiplication and division share the same rank and are worked left to right: 36 / 6 = 6, then 6 x 2 = 12. PEMDAS has four tiers, not six.

activities.title: Highlight the Layers
activities.instructions:
1. Students highlight the innermost parentheses in one color and the outer brackets in the second color.
2. Rule: you may only compute inside the innermost color still standing; when a layer collapses to one number, cross out its highlights.
3. Work three expressions; on the last one, students narrate the layer order aloud before touching any numbers.
4. Debrief question: what tells you a layer is finished?

activities.title: Inside-Out Relay
activities.instructions:
1. Each group gets a nested expression like 100 - [4 x (3 + 2) + 30].
2. Relay rule: each student computes exactly ONE step, rewrites the full line, and passes the board.
3. If a teammate spots an out-of-order step, they say 'layer check!' and the team talks before continuing.
4. First group to a correct final answer with every line true wins; any skipped rewrite voids the run.

strategy_links.why: Keisha's multiply-before-divide work is the canonical find-and-fix for this skill's central misconception.
Narrating the inside-out scan -- 'innermost layer, division first, sweep left to right' -- makes the invisible plan audible.
One-step-per-line whiteboard rounds expose exactly which layer or rank a student breaks first.

questioning_prompts: Which grouping symbols are innermost? Point to the layer you must finish first.
You have a division and a multiplication in the same line. Which one goes first, and what decides that?
Rewrite the expression after that step. Did the brackets survive, or did they collapse to a number?
If PEMDAS were written as four tiers instead of six letters, what would the tiers be?
Where would the answer change if the brackets disappeared? Test it.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes every multiplication before any division because M comes before D in PEMDAS.
misconception_redirects.say: Multiplication and division are the same step. When both appear, sweep left to right like reading. Put your finger on the leftmost x or / and do that one first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You swept left to right through the same-rank operations. That's the rule most people miss.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student works the outer brackets before finishing the inner parentheses, or mixes numbers from different layers.
misconception_redirects.say: Highlight the innermost parentheses. Nothing outside that highlight exists until the inside collapses to a single number.
misconception_redirects.praise: Inside out, layer by layer -- your work reads like a proof.

quick_checks.prompt: No solving -- just the first step of [(24 / 6 + 8) / 2].
quick_checks.look_for: '24 / 6.' An answer of '6 + 8' means ranking inside grouping is off; '8 / 2' means the layers are being read outside-in.
25 (20 / 4 = 5, then 5 x 5). An answer of 1 is the multiply-first error -- the canonical bug in one breath.

sentence_starters: The innermost layer is ___, so I start there.
Multiplication and division are the same rank, so I sweep left to right and do ___ first.

steps.annotation: Two layers: parentheses inside brackets. Start at the innermost layer.
Inside the parentheses, division beats addition: 54 / 9 = 6.
Finish the inner layer: 6 + 14 = 20. The parentheses collapse to one number.
Now the brackets' own division runs: 20 / 4 = 5.
Innermost layer first, and inside it multiplication beats subtraction: 5 x 8 = 40.
Finish the inside of the parentheses and rewrite the line.
Run the last division to collapse the brackets.

skills.name: Evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents and rational numbers
skills.i_do_script: Now the expressions bring in exponents and let fractions and decimals join the numbers. Watch me evaluate 3² + (4/5) x 10. The little 2 means 3 multiplied by ITSELF: 3 x 3 = 9 -- never 3 x 2. Exponents come right after grouping symbols in the order. Then (4/5) x 10 = 8, and 9 + 8 = 17. Same rules as always, one new player: the exponent.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the base by the exponent instead of by itself
canonical_error.example: Computes 3² as 3 x 2 = 6 instead of 3 x 3 = 9
canonical_error.why: The superscript looks like just another factor sitting next to the 3, so the student applies the operation they know -- multiplication by that number. They haven't internalized that the exponent COUNTS the copies of the base, it never joins the multiplication itself.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- the little number is a counter, not a factor.
redirect_script.prompt: Write the exponent out long before computing: 3² means 3 x 3. Write the expanded form under it, then multiply.
redirect_script.praise: You expanded the power before computing -- that habit makes exponents error-proof.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression combining a whole-number exponent (including zero) with fractions or decimals and one set of grouping symbols. Student evaluates. NR response; answers may be fractions or decimals.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 14 from 3² = 6; 3 46/5 from adding 3² + 4/5 first
Common errors: 0 from 5² = 10 (10 - 10); 90 from subtracting first (22.5 x 4)
Common errors: 9 from 2³ = 6 (6 x 1 1/2); 8 1/2 from multiplying 2³ x 1 then adding 1/2
Common errors: 4.5 from 4² = 8; 12.5 requires finishing the parentheses first (3.5), then 16 - 3.5

vocabulary.definition: The small raised number that counts how many copies of the base are multiplied together. In 3², the exponent is 2.
The number being repeatedly multiplied. In 3², the base is 3.
The whole package of base and exponent: 3² is read 'three to the second power' or 'three squared.'
Any nonzero number to the zero power equals 1: 6⁰ = 1.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S5 (equivalent expressions with the distributive property), then 6NS5-S6 to build and verify equivalent expressions yourself.
next_steps.if_fail: If the exponent is the failure point, drill expand-then-compute on bare powers. If fractions/decimals are the failure point, revisit 6NS5-F2.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 3² + (4/5) x 10.
Three jobs in this expression: an exponent, a fraction times a whole number, and an addition. Which does the order of operations send us to first -- and is there any grouping to check before that?
The parentheses just hold the fraction 4/5 -- nothing to compute inside. So the exponent is first. What does 3² actually MEAN, written out long?
If the student says 6, they multiplied 3 x 2. Ask: 'Is the little 2 one of the numbers being multiplied, or is it counting something? What is it counting?' Have them write 3 x 3 before computing.
So 3² = 3 x 3 = 9. Rewrite the line. What's next: the multiplication or the addition?
(4/5) x 10 -- what is four fifths of 10?
8. The line is now 9 + 8. Final answer?
17. The exponent slots in right after grouping symbols -- and it always means copies of the base, never times-the-little-number.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: 2³
Evaluate: 3² + 1
Evaluate: 4² + 3 x 2
practice_problems.notes: Exponent, then multiplication, then addition. Watch for 4² = 8 and for adding 16 + 3 first.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: 6² - 2.5 x 4
practice_problems.notes: The decimal multiplication (10) must finish before the subtraction.

practice_problems.stem: Andre evaluated 3² + 5. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 14. The exponent counts copies of the base: 3² = 3 x 3 = 9, so 9 + 5 = 14.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the base-times-exponent error. Have students write the expanded form 3 x 3 before computing.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: (1/2)² + 3/4
practice_problems.notes: (1/2)² = 1/4. Watch for (1/2)² = 1 (from 1/2 x 2) -- the same canonical error in fraction clothes.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate: 2 x (3² - 4) + 6⁰
practice_problems.notes: Exponent inside the parentheses first (9 - 4 = 5), and 6⁰ = 1, not 0 and not 6.
Two groupings feeding one multiplication: (8 - 3) x 2.

activities.title: Power Match-Up
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Partners match each power to its value -- but the decoy cards (the base-times-exponent answers) match nothing.
3. For every match, the matcher must say the expanded form aloud: '2³ is 2 times 2 times 2.'
4. Close: why were 6 and 8 sitting in the decoy pile? Whose wrong answers are they?

activities.title: Fix Andre's Exponent
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Andre's work and write the exact step where it broke.
2. They must fix it by writing the expanded form (3 x 3) before recomputing.
3. Then they build the counterexample: for which special base does Andre's method accidentally give the right answer? (2² -- because 2 x 2 and 2 + 2 and 2 x 2 all collide.)
4. Share out one-sentence tips that start 'The little number counts...'

content.error_step: Andre multiplied the base by the exponent -- he treated the little 2 as a factor.
content.why: The exponent counts how many copies of the base get multiplied: 3² = 3 x 3 = 9, so the answer is 14. (Sneaky fact: with base 2 the error is invisible, since 2 x 2 = 4 either way -- which is exactly why it survives so long.)

activities.title: Expand-It Choral Sprint
activities.instructions:
1. Flash a power (7²). The class answers in chorus with the EXPANDED form first ('7 times 7!'), then the value ('49!').
2. Two-beat rhythm: expand, then evaluate. No value may be spoken before its expansion.
3. Sprinkle in zero exponents (9⁰) and fraction bases ((1/2)²).
4. Any hesitation or split answer sends the card to the back of the deck for a second lap.

strategy_links.why: Building 3² as a 3-by-3 array of tiles (concrete) before the notation makes 'copies of the base' visible, not verbal.
Andre's 3 x 2 work -- and the sneaky base-2 case where the error hides -- is a rich find-and-fix discussion.
The expand-then-evaluate choral rhythm automates the habit that blocks the base-times-exponent bug.

questioning_prompts: What does the little raised number COUNT? Say it before you compute anything.
Write 5² out the long way before you evaluate it. Now which order-of-operations tier does it belong to?
Why does 2² hide the times-the-exponent mistake, while 3² exposes it?
What is 6⁰, and why isn't it 0 or 6?
In 4² - (6 - 2.5), what runs first -- the exponent or the parentheses? What rule says so?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student computes 3² as 3 x 2 = 6, or (1/2)² as 1.
misconception_redirects.say: Write the exponent out long before computing: 3² means 3 x 3. Write the expanded form under it, then multiply.
misconception_redirects.praise: You expanded the power before computing -- that habit makes exponents error-proof.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student evaluates the exponent last, or lets the addition run before the multiplication in a line like 9 + (4/5) x 10.
misconception_redirects.say: Rebuild the order: grouping symbols, then exponents, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract. Label each piece of the expression with its tier number before computing.
misconception_redirects.praise: You gave every operation its correct turn -- that's the full order of operations at work.

quick_checks.prompt: Quick: is 5² equal to 10 or 25? Say the expanded form that proves it.
quick_checks.look_for: '25, because 5² is 5 x 5.' An answer of 10 -- or a correct 25 with no expansion -- means the counter-vs-factor idea isn't anchored.
1. Answers of 0 or 8 signal the zero-exponent convention (explicitly in scope for this standard) hasn't landed.

sentence_starters: The exponent counts ___ copies of ___, so I write ___ before computing.
After grouping symbols, the next tier is ___, so I evaluate ___ first.

steps.annotation: Check grouping first -- the parentheses just hold the fraction, nothing to compute. Exponents come next.
3² means 3 x 3 = 9. Never 3 x 2 -- the little 2 counts copies.
Multiplication before addition: 4/5 of 10 is 8.
The addition goes last.
Exponent first: 5² = 5 x 5 = 25.
Multiplication beats subtraction -- compute 2.5 x 4 and rewrite the line.
Finish with the subtraction.

skills.name: Apply the distributive property to write equivalent expressions
skills.i_do_script: In S2 you NAMED the distributive property; now you'll USE it to rewrite an expression without changing its value. Watch: 6(8 + 5) means six copies of the whole package, so the 6 multiplies BOTH terms: 6 x 8 + 6 x 5 = 48 + 30 = 78. Check it the other way: 6 x 13 = 78. Same value, new outfit. The 6 never skips a term inside its parentheses -- and it never reaches terms outside them.

canonical_error.pattern: Distributes to only the first term inside the parentheses, or distributes to terms OUTSIDE the parentheses
canonical_error.example: Rewrites 7(9 + 4) as 7 x 9 + 4 = 67 instead of 7 x 9 + 7 x 4 = 91; or rewrites 8(16 + 24) - 52 as (8 x 16) + (8 x 24) - (8 x 52)
canonical_error.why: The student sees the multiplication touching the first number and stops -- they don't picture 7(9 + 4) as seven COPIES of the whole (9 + 4) package. The overreach error is the same misunderstanding inverted: they don't see that the parentheses mark exactly where the multiplier's reach ends.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- did the multiplier reach every term it should, and none it shouldn't?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw an arrow from the outside number to EACH term inside the parentheses -- every term gets its own arrow, and nothing outside the parentheses gets one. Then check by evaluating both versions.
redirect_script.praise: Every inside term got the multiplier and the outside stayed untouched -- and you proved it with a value check.

skills.item_template: A numerical expression of the form a(b + c) or a(b - c), possibly with an extra term outside the parentheses. Student selects or writes the equivalent expression, or evaluates using the property. MC or NR response.

sample_items.stem:
An expression is given.

8(16 + 24) - 52

Which expression is equivalent to the given expression?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The third choice is the overreach error -- distributing the 8 to the 52 outside the parentheses; the first two turn multiplication into addition
5 x 9 + 3 is the first-term-only error; the others swap multiplication and addition
Common error: 4 x 7 + 2 -- the 4 skips the second term
Common error: 6 x 10 - 3; also watch for adding when the inside is a subtraction

sample_items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 3 x 12 + 3 x 8?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Factoring direction: 6 x (12 + 8) double-counts the 3; the others merge operations wrongly

sample_items.stem: Use the distributive property: 7 x 98 = 7 x (100 - 2). What is the value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common error: 700 - 2 = 698 -- the 7 skips the second term
9 x 20 + 4 is the first-term-only error

sample_items.stem: Fill in the blank: 5 x (8 + 6) = 5 x 8 + 5 x ___
sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 30 (writes the product instead of the term), 8 (repeats the first term)
The third choice is the overreach error -- the 2 reaching the 10 outside its parentheses

sample_items.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 12 x 7 + 12 x 3?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Factoring direction with a friendly check: both equal 120

vocabulary.definition: A number multiplying a parentheses package multiplies EVERY term inside: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c.
Expressions that are worth the same value even though they're written differently.
One of the pieces being added or subtracted. In 9 + 4, the terms are 9 and 4.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6NS5-S6: build multiple equivalent expressions and place grouping symbols to hit a target value.
next_steps.if_fail: Return to 6NS5-S2 to solidify what the property CLAIMS, then re-teach with the arrows-and-value-check routine.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: Which expression is equivalent to 8(16 + 24) - 52?
No sign between the 8 and the parenthesis -- what operation is hiding there, and what exactly is the 8 multiplying?
8(16 + 24) means eight copies of the whole package (16 + 24). Which terms does the 8 have to reach -- and is the 52 one of them?
Draw an arrow from the 8 to the 16 and a second arrow from the 8 to the 24. The 52 sits OUTSIDE the parentheses, so it gets no arrow. Write: 8 x 16 + 8 x 24 - 52.

If the student also multiplies the 52 and writes (8 x 16) + (8 x 24) - (8 x 52), an arrow reached a term it never should. Ask: 'Is the 52 inside the parentheses or outside? Where does the 8's reach stop?' The closing parenthesis is the fence -- the 8 never crosses it.
Now prove the two forms match. Take the original the short way: what's 16 + 24, then 8 times that, then minus 52?
And the distributed form: what's 8 x 16, plus 8 x 24, minus 52?

268 both ways, so (8 x 16) + (8 x 24) - 52 is the equivalent expression. Distributing the 8 to the 52 as well would subtract 416 instead of 52 -- way too much. The value check is how you PROVE equivalence, every time.

practice_problems.stem: Rewrite 3(4 + 5) using the distributive property.
Evaluate 2 x (10 + 3). Then evaluate 2 x 10 + 2 x 3. Are they equal?
Which expression is equivalent to 6(8 + 5): '6 x 8 + 5' or '6 x 8 + 6 x 5'? Prove it with values.
practice_problems.notes: The value check is the point -- require both computations.

practice_problems.stem: Use the distributive property to evaluate 4 x 27 by rewriting it as 4 x (20 + 7).
practice_problems.notes: The property as a mental-math tool, the way Number Talks use it.

practice_problems.stem: Ava rewrote 7(9 + 4) using the distributive property. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 7 x 9 + 7 x 4 = 63 + 28 = 91. The 7 multiplies BOTH terms inside the parentheses. Check: 7 x 13 = 91, not 67.
practice_problems.notes: First-term-only bait. Arrows from the 7 to EACH term, then the value check.

practice_problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 5 x 14 + 5 x 6?
practice_problems.notes: Factoring direction -- pulling the common 5 back out.

practice_problems.stem: Write two different expressions equivalent to 6 x (10 + 5).
practice_problems.answer: e.g. 6 x 10 + 6 x 5, and 6 x 15 (or (10 + 5) x 6). All equal 90.
practice_problems.notes: Producing multiple forms previews S6.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why (8 x 16) + (8 x 24) - (8 x 52) is NOT equivalent to 8(16 + 24) - 52.
practice_problems.answer: The 8 only multiplies the terms inside its parentheses -- 16 and 24. The 52 is outside, so it is subtracted as-is. Multiplying it by 8 subtracts too much (416 instead of 52).
practice_problems.notes: The overreach error from the ILEARN-style item, explained in words.

activities.title: Distribute-and-Match
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards. Partners match each a(b + c) expression to its correctly distributed form.
2. Two decoys are first-term-only rewrites (like 5 x 9 + 3) that match nothing.
3. Every match must be proved with one value check spoken aloud.
4. Close: what do both decoys have in common? (The multiplier skipped the second term.)

activities.title: Where Did Ava's 28 Go?
activities.instructions:
1. Groups examine Ava's rewrite of 7(9 + 4) and compute BOTH versions before discussing.
2. The numbers disagree (67 vs 91) -- so the group's job is to find which term never got multiplied.
3. Redraw the problem with arrows from the 7 to each inside term.
4. Exit prompt: finish the sentence 'The parentheses tell the multiplier exactly...'

content.error_step: Ava distributed the 7 to the first term only -- the 4 never got multiplied.
content.why: 7(9 + 4) means seven copies of the WHOLE package, so both terms get the 7: 7 x 9 + 7 x 4 = 91. The check 7 x 13 = 91 confirms it; Ava's 67 fails the check.

activities.title: Mental-Math Number Talk: Friendly Splits
activities.instructions:
1. Pose 6 x 98 with no pencils allowed.
2. Collect answers first, then strategies. Steer toward the split: 6 x (100 - 2) = 600 - 12 = 588.
3. Repeat with 4 x 27 and 8 x 53, having students name the split BEFORE computing: '8 x (50 + 3).'
4. Debrief: the distributive property is the reason the trick works -- write each spoken strategy in property notation.

strategy_links.why: Number Talks make the distributive property the student's own mental-math strategy instead of a rule to memorize.
A correct distribution next to Ava's first-term-only version turns the value check into the lesson.
Model the arrows routine, distribute one together, then release -- the skill is a procedure that benefits from staged handoff.

questioning_prompts: What operation hides between the 8 and the parenthesis in 8(16 + 24)?
How many terms live inside the parentheses? Did each one get its own arrow from the multiplier?
Evaluate the original and evaluate your rewrite. Do they match? What does a mismatch tell you?
The 52 sits outside the parentheses in 8(16 + 24) - 52. Why doesn't the 8 touch it?
How could the distributive property make 7 x 98 easy to do in your head?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student rewrites 7(9 + 4) as 7 x 9 + 4, or lets the multiplier reach a term outside the parentheses.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw an arrow from the outside number to EACH term inside the parentheses -- every term gets its own arrow, and nothing outside the parentheses gets one. Then check by evaluating both versions.
misconception_redirects.praise: Every inside term got the multiplier and the outside stayed untouched -- and you proved it with a value check.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student turns the multiplication into addition -- rewrites 5(9 + 3) as (5 + 9) x (5 + 3).
misconception_redirects.say: Read the original out loud: 'five TIMES the package.' The 5 multiplies; it never gets added to anything. Write the two arrows and keep the x signs.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the operations straight -- the multiplier multiplies, full stop.

quick_checks.look_for: 3 x 10 + 3 x 6 (or 30 + 18). '3 x 10 + 6' means the first-term-only error is live -- ask them to value-check both forms.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: 4(5 + 2) - 3 is equivalent to 4 x 5 + 4 x 2 - 4 x 3.
quick_checks.look_for: False, because the 3 is outside the parentheses -- the 8's... the 4's reach ends at the closing parenthesis. 'True' is the overreach error.

sentence_starters: The ___ multiplies EVERY term inside, so I write ___ + ___.
I proved they're equivalent because both versions equal ___.

steps.annotation: The 8 multiplies the whole package (16 + 24). The 52 sits OUTSIDE the parentheses.
Distribute: the 8 reaches each term inside -- and stops at the closing parenthesis. The 52 stays as it was.
Both forms equal 268, so they're equivalent. The wrong version 8 x 52 would have subtracted 416 -- way too much.

faded_example.stem: Rewrite 9(20 + 4) using the distributive property, then evaluate both forms to check.

steps.math: 9(20 + 4): the 9 multiplies BOTH the 20 and the 4
steps.annotation: Draw an arrow from the 9 to each term inside.
Write the distributed form with both products.
Evaluate both forms -- the original the short way (9 x 24) and your rewrite -- and confirm they match.

skills.name: Create equivalent expressions and place grouping symbols for a target value
skills.i_do_script: Now we run the whole standard in reverse: instead of evaluating an expression someone else wrote, YOU decide where the grouping symbols go, or judge which of several expressions are worth the same amount. Watch: make 4 x 3 + 5 = 32 true with one set of parentheses. Without them it's 12 + 5 = 17 -- no. Try 4 x (3 + 5): that's 4 x 8 = 32 -- yes. Every placement is a guess you must CHECK by evaluating.

canonical_error.pattern: Places grouping symbols (or accepts an 'equivalent' expression) without evaluating to check the value
canonical_error.example: Asked to make 2 x 8 - 5 = 6 true, writes (2 x 8) - 5, which equals 11, and moves on without checking against the 6
canonical_error.why: The student treats parentheses as decoration to be added anywhere rather than as a move that CHANGES the value. They stop at 'I placed the symbols' instead of closing the loop: evaluate the new expression and compare it to the target.

redirect_script.stop: You placed them -- but did you check them?
redirect_script.prompt: Evaluate your new expression all the way down to one number, then compare it to the target. If it doesn't match, move the parentheses to a different pair of numbers and check again.
redirect_script.praise: You treated it as guess-and-CHECK -- placing symbols and proving the value. That's the full job.

skills.item_template: Either (a) a multi-select: choose all expressions equivalent to a given one, or (b) an equation missing one set of parentheses: student places them to make it true. MS or NR response.

sample_items.stem: Select the three expressions that are equivalent to (14 - 8) x 4 x 9.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The original equals 216. 10 x 9 = 90 comes from subtracting 14 - 8 wrong or adding; 28 x 9 = 252 comes from ignoring the parentheses (14 - 8 x 4 misread)

sample_items.stem:
Place one set of parentheses in the equation to make it true.

4 x 3 + 5 = 32
sample_items.distractor_logic: Without parentheses the value is 17. Students who don't check may leave (4 x 3) + 5, which changes nothing

sample_items.stem:
Place one set of parentheses in the equation to make it true.

20 - 8 / 4 = 3
sample_items.distractor_logic: Without parentheses the value is 18. The parentheses must force the subtraction to run first

sample_items.stem: Select all expressions that are equivalent to 5 x (6 + 2).
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5 x 6 + 2 and 30 + 2 both equal 32 -- the first-term-only distribution error in two disguises; the correct pair both equal 40

vocabulary.definition: Expressions that are worth the same value even though they're written differently.
Parentheses ( ) or brackets [ ] that force the part inside to be computed first.
The number your expression must equal after you place the grouping symbols.

next_steps.if_pass: The student owns this standard forward and backward -- ready for 7.NS work with all four operations on rational numbers (7.NS.3, 7.NS.4).
next_steps.if_fail: If placements are wrong but checked, review how parentheses change order (6NS5-S1/S3). If placements go unchecked, drill the evaluate-and-compare loop before anything else.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: Place one set of parentheses to make this true: 4 x 3 + 5 = 32.
First, what is 4 x 3 + 5 worth right now, with no parentheses? Evaluate it.
17, not 32. So the parentheses must CHANGE something. What are the only two places one set of parentheses could go?
Try (4 x 3) + 5 first. Evaluate it. Did anything change? Why not?
Right -- those parentheses just repeat what order of operations already did. Parentheses only matter when they OVERRIDE the normal order.
Now try 4 x (3 + 5). Evaluate it. Does it hit the target?
If the student writes the parentheses and stops, ask: 'How do you KNOW it's 32 now? Show me the check.' The evaluate-and-compare step is the skill -- don't accept placement without proof.
4 x 8 = 32 -- checked and true. Placement is a guess; the check is what makes it an answer.

practice_problems.stem: Evaluate (10 - 4) x 2 and 10 - 4 x 2. Are they equal?
Is 3 x (4 + 6) equivalent to 3 x 10? How do you know?
Place one set of parentheses in 6 + 4 x 5 = 50 to make it true.
practice_problems.notes: Without parentheses it's 26. The check against 50 is required.

practice_problems.stem: Place one set of parentheses in 36 / 3 + 3 = 6 to make it true.
practice_problems.notes: Without parentheses it's 15. Parentheses must capture the addition under the division.

practice_problems.stem: Tia was asked to place one set of parentheses in 2 x 8 - 5 = 6 to make it true. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 2 x (8 - 5) = 6. Tia never compared her value to the target: 11 is not 6. Placing parentheses is guess-and-CHECK -- the value must match the target before you're done.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the place-without-checking error. Note her parentheses also changed nothing -- they repeated the default order.

practice_problems.stem: Which expressions are equivalent to (12 - 4) x 3: '8 x 3', '24', '12 - 4 x 3', '12 - 12'?
practice_problems.answer: 8 x 3 and 24. The other two equal 0 -- without the parentheses, the multiplication runs first.
practice_problems.notes: Multi-select judgment with the no-parentheses foil.

practice_problems.stem: Place one set of parentheses in 5 + 3 x 2 + 4 = 23 to make it true.
practice_problems.notes: Three candidate spots; only one survives the check (3 x 6 = 18, plus 5 = 23).

practice_problems.stem: Write two different expressions equivalent to 4 x (5 + 3), each using a different property or form. Name the move you used.
practice_problems.answer: e.g. 4 x 5 + 4 x 3 (distributive property) and (5 + 3) x 4 (commutative property); all equal 32.
practice_problems.notes: Producing equivalents and naming the property closes the loop with S2 and S5.

activities.title: Tia's Unchecked Parentheses
activities.instructions:
1. Show Tia's work. First question: is her arithmetic wrong, or is something else wrong? (Her arithmetic is fine -- 16 - 5 IS 11.)
2. Groups name the missing step: comparing 11 to the target 6.
3. Groups fix it by testing the other placement, 2 x (8 - 5), and checking against 6.
4. Debrief: her parentheses also changed nothing about the order. When do parentheses actually matter?

content.worked_problem: Make 2 x 8 - 5 = 6 true with one set of parentheses. Tia wrote: (2 x 8) - 5 = 11. Done!
content.error_step: Tia stopped after placing the symbols -- she never compared her value (11) to the target (6).
content.why: The job has two halves: place, then CHECK. 2 x (8 - 5) = 2 x 3 = 6 hits the target; Tia's placement also merely repeated the default order, so it couldn't change anything.

activities.title: Equivalent or Impostor?
materials: Expression cards keyed to (14 - 8) x 4 x 9
activities.instructions:
1. Write the anchor expression (14 - 8) x 4 x 9 on the board and evaluate it together: 216.
2. Partners sort each card as 'Equivalent (= 216)' or 'Impostor.'
3. Rule: no card is placed without saying its value aloud.
4. Debrief on 28 x 9 -- which exact order-of-operations mistake produces it? (Ignoring the parentheses: 14 - 8 x 4 read as multiplication first... then mis-grouped.)

activities.title: Parentheses Golf
activities.instructions:
1. Each 'hole' is an equation missing its parentheses, like 6 + 4 x 5 = 50.
2. Partner A places one set of parentheses -- that's the swing. Partner B evaluates the result -- that's the scorecard. A placement that hits the target scores in one; each miss is another stroke.
3. Swap roles each hole. Lowest total strokes after 5 holes wins.
4. House rule: an unchecked placement counts as two strokes -- checking IS the game.

content.worked_problem: Hole example: 6 + 4 x 5 = 50. Swing: (6 + 4) x 5. Check: 10 x 5 = 50. Hole in one.
content.error_step: A swing without a check -- writing parentheses and calling it done.
content.why: Parentheses change the value; only evaluating proves the target is hit.

strategy_links.why: Sharing the different splits of 216 (6 x 36, 24 x 9, 54 x 4) is a natural Number Talk about equivalent forms.
Place-then-check invites a think-pair-share: my placement, your check, our verdict.
Tia's unchecked placement is the exact habit-level error this skill exists to fix.

questioning_prompts: Before placing anything: what is the expression worth with NO parentheses? Is that already the target?
How many different places could one set of parentheses go here? List them before you pick.
You placed your parentheses -- what's the value now, and does it match the target?
Why did (4 x 3) + 5 change nothing? When do parentheses actually change a value?
These two expressions use the same numbers. Does that make them equivalent? What's the only test that counts?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student places parentheses (or selects an 'equivalent' expression) and moves on without evaluating to compare.
misconception_redirects.say: Evaluate your new expression all the way down to one number, then compare it to the target. If it doesn't match, move the parentheses to a different pair of numbers and check again.
misconception_redirects.praise: You treated it as guess-and-CHECK -- placing symbols and proving the value. That's the full job.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student assumes two expressions are equivalent because they contain the same numbers in the same order.
misconception_redirects.say: Same numbers is not the test -- same VALUE is. Evaluate both expressions completely and put the two results side by side.
misconception_redirects.praise: You judged by value, not by looks. That's what equivalent means.

quick_checks.prompt: One set of parentheses in 10 - 6 / 2 to make it equal 2. Go.
quick_checks.look_for: (10 - 6) / 2 = 2, WITH the check spoken. Placing 10 - (6 / 2) = 7 and stopping means the check loop still isn't closed.

quick_checks.prompt: Is 24 x 9 equivalent to (14 - 8) x 4 x 9? Prove it in one line.
quick_checks.look_for: Yes: (14 - 8) x 4 = 24, so both are 24 x 9 = 216. A 'yes' without values is pattern-matching, not proof.

They are equivalent because BOTH expressions equal ___.

worked_solution.stem: Place one set of parentheses in the equation to make it true: 4 x 3 + 5 = 32

steps.annotation: First find the value with NO parentheses. 17 is not 32, so the parentheses must change the order.
These parentheses repeat what order of operations already does -- nothing changes. Cross this option off.
These parentheses OVERRIDE the order: addition now runs first. Evaluate and compare to the target.
The check against the target is what turns a guess into an answer.

faded_example.stem: Place one set of parentheses in 6 + 4 x 5 = 50 to make it true.

steps.annotation: 26 is not 50, so the parentheses must change which step runs first.
There are two candidate placements. Try one, evaluate it completely.
Compare your value to the target 50. If it misses, try the other placement and check again.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (nested grouping, the approaching-proficiency band). If the student passes, probe S4 (exponents with rationals) and S6 (create/place).
